extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and literary critics interested in the formal aspects of fantasy and prophetic fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for producing or judging two modes of the novel — the fantastic (fantasy) and the prophetic — covering devices, tone, characterization, and readerly demands. Uses examples (Flecker’s Magic, Zuleika Dobson, Tristram Shandy, Ulysses, George Eliot, Dostoevsky) to illustrate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy implies (or suggests) the supernatural
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-served fantasy 'implies the supernatural, but need not express it.' The supernatural can be explicit or merely lurking as a suggestion beneath the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work may be classed as fantasy even when the deity or supernatural principle is only implicit (e.g., Tristram Shandy’s hidden 'Muddle'). The implication alone can create the fantastic atmosphere without literal manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognisable devices of the fantastic
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers of a fantastic turn habitually use a limited set of devices: the introduction of a god, ghost, angel, monkey, monster, midget, witch into ordinary life; introduction of ordinary men into no man’s land, the future, the past, the interior of the earth, the fourth dimension; divings into and dividings of personality; and parody or adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices 'need never grow stale' because temperament and fresh handling renew them. Authors should select and manipulate these limited devices rather than invent wholly new mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merging magic and common sense in diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The true fantasist 'merges the kingdoms of magic and common sense by using words that apply to both,' letting language operate in dual senses so the mixture comes alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words and images that are simultaneously plausible in everyday reality and resonant with the supernatural; this linguistic double-meaning animates the fantasy (example: the phrasing of Flecker’s wishes). Avoid purely ornamental fantasy diction that cannot be read on two levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite, individual characterization to 'grip' the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in fantasy, 'his character, though slightly sketched, is individual, and this definiteness causes the book to grip.' Specificity of character anchors the fantastic events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create distinct, individualized protagonists whose concrete wants and confusions make the fantastic consequences emotionally compelling. Without such definiteness the fantasy risks drifting into mere whimsy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative method and pacing in fantasy (Socratic/gradual tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy may proceed 'with a growing tension, a series of little shocks' and in the example given the method is 'Socratic' (questioning progression of increasingly fraught wishes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the fantastic scenario as a sequence of escalating dilemmas or revelations. Small shocks and iterative questioning can maintain reader engagement rather than a single, flat magical premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and adaptation as a practical technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody or adaptation allows the fantasist to adopt an earlier work or tradition as mythology or framework, supplying patterns and cornices for invention and helping writers who struggle to create characters from scratch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing or reshaping an existing narrative world (e.g., Fielding’s play on Pamela, Lowes Dickinson’s use of Mozart, Joyce’s use of the Odyssey) can provide structural scaffolding. Beware the 'false start' where parody becomes seriousness without coherence (Joseph Andrews example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy’s characteristic relation to confusion and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy’s confusion is fundamental and playful: it 'glances about' and is prone to changing mythologies and devices (e.g., Zuleika Dobson’s shifting mythology); the genre tolerates multiplicity rather than single-minded unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept episodic, kaleidoscopic structures and shifts of mythology as inherent strengths of fantasy, but manage them so the reader can follow the imaginative play. Avoid incoherence that undermines engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy as a tone of voice (accent) rather than literal prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy here is 'a tone of voice' — an 'accent in the novelist’s voice' that implies larger faiths or cosmic meanings; it is expressed through the novelist’s phrasing rather than explicit foretelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an overarching tonal quality (a 'song') that pervades diction and phrase-turns; attend to the novelist’s state of mind and exact words. The prophetic mode depends on sustained vocal authority rather than plot contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic fiction demands readerly humility and suspension of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophetic aspect 'demands two qualities: humility and the suspension of the sense of humour.' Without humility the reader will laugh at the prophet and miss the voice; humour can distract from the prophetic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers aiming for a prophetic pitch should anticipate a reader who can accept exalted or solemn tone without irony; reviewers and readers should approach with openness. Conversely, if the audience lacks these qualities the work risks being treated as farcical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters in prophetic fiction extend to imply universality
rubrics_metrics.description: In prophetic work characters and situations 'stand for more than themselves' and 'expand to embrace' the infinite; individuals (e.g., Mitya) imply 'all of us' rather than just their own particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters whose particular choices and experiences carry metaphoric or universal resonance; the text should permit 'extension' where character instances evoke broader human conditions rather than merely serving local realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spasmodic/ intermittent realism within prophetic fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction is 'spasmodically realistic'—it can be patiently accurate about minute, domestic or procedural details even while engaged in immense visionary aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use close, detailed realism in foreground moments (trials, staircases, catalogues) to anchor the visionary passages, letting small factual precision sharpen the prophetic intensity rather than contradict it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic fiction produces a sensation of song and roughness of surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophetic voice 'gives us the sensation of a song or of sound' and is often characterized by 'roughness of surface'—dents, grooves and spikes that may be forgotten once the work settles into greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow stylistic roughness (uneven passages, violent metaphors) as part of a prophetic voice; the musical or bardic quality of language is more important than polished domestic smoothing. Aim for memorable tonal effects rather than uniform stylistic perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy or prophetic aspect tends toward unity rather than multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy's 'face is towards unity, whereas fantasy glances about'; its confusion is incidental, not fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cultivating a prophetic mode, organize thematic and tonal elements toward a sense of cohesion and overarching meaning. Avoid treating prophetic material as an assemblage of disparate mythologies (the opposite tendency of fantasy).
